<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    To maximize the impact of precision medicine approaches, it is critical to identify genetic variants underlying disease and to accurately quantify their functional effects. A gene exemplifying the challenge of variant interpretation is the von Hippel–Lindautumor suppressor (
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    ).
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase that regulates the cellular response to hypoxia. Germline pathogenic variants in
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    predispose patients to tumors including clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) and pheochromocytoma, and somatic
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    mutations are frequently observed in sporadic renal cancer. Here we optimize and apply saturation genome editing to assay nearly all possible single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) across
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    ’s coding sequence. To delineate mechanisms, we quantify mRNA dosage effects and compare functional effects in isogenic cell lines. Function scores for 2,268
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    SNVs identify a core set of pathogenic alleles driving ccRCC with perfect accuracy, inform differential risk across tumor types and reveal new mechanisms by which variants impact function. These results have immediate utility for classifying
                    <jats:italic>VHL</jats:italic>
                    variants encountered clinically and illustrate how precise functional measurements can resolve pleiotropic and dosage-dependent genotype–phenotype relationships across complete genes.
                  </jats:p>
title: Saturation genome editing maps the functional spectrum of pathogenic VHL alleles
